notes.short: “Martha, Martha”: her name said twice, in earnest
notes.about: When Martha asks the Lord to send Mary to help her, He answers by saying her name twice. The doubled name is emphatic: it calls attention to her and to what He says next, about her worry over many things. It can also voice His tender care for her as He gently corrects her.

figure.name: Epizeuxis
figure.words: Martha, Martha
figure.means: an earnest, emphatic call to Martha, which can also voice His care for her

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse among the doubled names in Figures of Speech, where the figure draws special attention to the person and the words. Henry says the Lord repeated her name as one in earnest, concerned for her good. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it an emphatic doubling. Plumptre (Ellicott) finds special tenderness in the reproof it carries.

cites.quote: Seven of these are used by God to man (four of which are in the Old Testament, and three in the New), the other three being used under other circumstances. When thus used, the figure calls special attention to the occasion or to the person, and to some solemn moment of importance in the action, or of significance in the words. ... Martha, Martha (Luk 10:41).
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: When he reproved her, he called her by her name, Martha; for reproofs are then most likely to do good when they are particular, applied to particular persons and cases, as Nathan's to David, Thou art the man. He repeated her name, Martha, Martha; he speaks as one in earnest, and deeply concerned for her welfare.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: emphatically redoubling upon the name.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: We note a special tenderness of reproof in the two-fold utterance of the name
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Side by side: Martha serves, Mary listens
notes.about: Luke sets the two sisters side by side. Martha welcomes Jesus and works hard to serve Him, but is worried and upset; Mary sits at His feet and listens. Jesus does not fault Martha’s welcome, but says Mary has chosen the good portion.

sides.label: Serves Him, but is anxious
sides.words: you are worried and upset about many things

sides.label: Sits at His feet and listens
sides.words: Mary has chosen the good portion

notes.evidence: Henry says Martha’s work was good in its season, yet Christ blamed her for not doing as Mary did. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls both true-hearted disciples, in the higher and the lower of two ways of honouring the Lord. Clarke: she erred only through love for the Lord; Martha was well employed, Mary better. Augustine, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas: not a bad part, but a better.
notes.limit: Martha is not set aside: her care came from love for the Lord, her work was good in its place, and John 11:5 says Jesus loved her. The writers differ on how far her anxious care was at fault.

cites.quote: Martha's care and work were good in their proper season and place; but now she had something else to do, which was unspeakably more needful, and therefore should be done first, and most minded. She expected Christ to have blamed Mary for not doing as she did, but he blamed her for not doing as Mary did
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Both were true-hearted disciples, but the one was absorbed in the higher, the other in the lower of two ways of honoring their common Lord. Yet neither despised, or would willingly neglect, the other's occupation.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Through her affectionate respect for our Lord and his disciples, and through that alone, she erred. There is not the slightest intimation that she was either worldly-minded or careless about her soul ... The utmost that can be said on the subject is, Martha was well employed, but Mary, on this occasion, better.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Our Lord then does not blame the actions, but distinguishes between the duties. For it follows, Mary hath chosen that good part, &c. Not thine a bad one, but hers a better.
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

notes.short: Four kinds of guests, named with no “and” in Greek
notes.about: Jesus names four kinds of guests. In Luke's Greek no “and” joins them (the BSB adds one before the last), so the list hurries on to the promise: “and you will be blessed.” When the master sends for the same four in 14:21, the Greek puts an “and” before each.

figure.name: Asyndeton
figure.words: the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind
figure.means: four kinds of guests passed over quickly, to reach the blessing promised in the next verse

original.note: In Luke's Greek the four words in 14:13 stand side by side with no “and”; in 14:21 kai, “and”, comes before each of them.

notes.evidence: Bullinger illustrates both figures with this pair, at the head of Polysyndeton: in verse 13 the four classes are named without “and”, so we are hastened on to the weighty conclusion, the blessing; in verse 21 an “and” before each detains us at every step.
notes.limit: The figure is in the Greek wording, which the BSB smooths: it adds an “and” before the last name in 14:13, and in 14:21 has only two where the Greek has four.

cites.quote: In verse 13, we have Asyndeton (no-ands): and in verse 21, Polysyndeton (many-ands). In the former case (Asyndeton) … we are hastened on to the important and weighty conclusion … we are hurried over the enumeration of these classes to be told of this blessing. … by the use of this figure of Polysyndeton in verse 21, we are not hurried on to any climax at the end, but we are detained at each step
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: “Hate” here means to love them less than Christ
notes.about: Jesus does not tell His followers to hate their families. The strong word says more than is meant literally: read with Matthew 10:37, it means loving father, mother and all the rest, even one's own life, less than Him. He must come first.

figure.name: Hyperbole
figure.words: hate
figure.means: to love them less than Christ, so that He comes before family and even one's own life

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Hyperbole: not to hate them is not to esteem them less than Christ. Henry says a disciple must comparatively hate his relations, loving them less than Christ, as Leah is said to be hated when Rachel was loved more. Clarke and Calvin read it by Matthew 10:37, Calvin noting that Luke's word is harsher but the meaning the same.
notes.limit: The word allows no ill will toward family and no neglect of duty to them. It sets the order of love, so that where their claims, or love of one's own life, stand against Christ, He comes first.

cites.quote: “If any man come to me and hate not his father and mother”: i.e., does not esteem them less than me. So the verb to hate is used
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Every good man loves his relations; and yet, if he be a disciple of Christ, he must comparatively hate them, must love them less than Christ, as Leah is said to be hated when Rachel was better loved. Not that their persons must be in any degree hated
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Matthew, Mat 10:37, expresses the true meaning of this word, when he says, He who loveth his father and mother More than me.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He does not indeed enjoin us to lay aside human affections, or forbid us to discharge the duties of relationship ... The phrase employed by Luke is more harsh, if any man doth not hate his father and mother, but the meaning is the same
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The son comes home; the father runs to meet him
notes.about: The son comes home, and nothing is said of haste; while he is still far off, his father sees him and runs to meet him. The two are set side by side, and the father's running shows how ready God is to receive a sinner who returns.

sides.label: Comes home, in no haste
sides.words: So he got up and went to his father.

sides.label: Runs to meet him
sides.words: He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the father's running is opposed to the way the son came: the son came slowly, the father ran; he reads the welcome as showing God's readiness to pity and pardon returning sinners. Henry likewise sets the son, coming slowly under shame and fear, beside the father who ran to meet him, and reads it as showing how quick God is to show mercy.
notes.limit: The verse does not say the son came slowly; the writers read it so, from his shame. He is not faulted for it: he is coming home to confess his sin (verse 21).

cites.quote: And ran - This is opposed to the manner in which the son came. The beauty of the picture is greatly heightened by these circumstances. The son came slowly - the father "ran." ... This is evidently designed to denote the "readiness of God" to pity and pardon returning sinners.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He ran. This denotes how swift God is to show mercy. The prodigal son came slowly, under a burden of shame and fear; but the tender father ran to meet him with his encouragements.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The father's welcome, told act by act with “and”
notes.about: The father's welcome is told act by act: he sees his son, is filled with compassion, runs, embraces him and kisses him. Told with “and” again and again, each act is weighed on its own, and together they show the fulness of God's grace to a sinner who returns.

figure.name: Polysyndeton
figure.words: his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.
figure.means: each act of the father's welcome, weighed on its own, showing the fulness of God's grace to the sinner who returns

original.note: In Luke's Greek kai, and, links the father's acts more often than the BSB shows.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Polysyndeton: the five acts of the father, joined by and, are to be dwelt on one by one, and together they show how full God's grace is in welcoming the lost sinner. He adds that they do not build to a climax.

cites.quote: five particulars give the fulness of Divine grace in receiving the lost sinner ... There is no climax; but we are asked to dwell separately on these five aspects of grace
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: Glory in the highest set against peace on earth
notes.about: The angels' song sets two clauses against each other: glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth. The highest heaven is set against the earth; if the words about men belong with peace on earth, God is set against men as well.

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men
figure.means: glory given to God in the highest heaven, set against peace given to men on earth

notes.evidence: Bullinger (Figures of Speech) lists the verse under Antithesis: glory in the highest to God, and on earth peace, with a third fact following from them. Bengel points out a double antithesis: in the highest set against on earth, and to God set against among men. Calvin says the two clauses match, and that God and men must be set clearly against each other for the contrast to show.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whether the song has two parts or three. Either way, the highest heaven is set against the earth.

cites.quote: “Glory in the highest to God, and on earth peace.” And then, after these two Antitheta, a third fact is stated as resulting from them when coming together
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Moreover we ought to observe the double antithesis: 1. between, in the highest, and, on earth; 2. between, to God, and, among men.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/luke/2.htm

cites.quote: The most general reading is, that the words, among men good-will, should stand as a third clause. ... but the other appears to be preferable. The two clauses, Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth, do unquestionably agree with each other; but if you do not place men and God in marked opposition, the contrast will not fully appear.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: A common saying: “Physician, heal yourself!”
notes.about: Jesus knows His hometown will throw a common saying at Him: “Physician, heal yourself!” They want Him to do among His own people the works they heard He did in Capernaum. He answers that “no prophet is accepted in his hometown” (verse 24).

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: Physician, heal yourself!
figure.means: do among your own people at home the healing works you have done for others elsewhere

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia and calls it a well known proverb. Barnes says it was probably in common use, here a demand that He show by miracles why they should trust Him. Calvin explains the common proverb as a physician beginning with his own people, and Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) likens it to our saying, charity begins at home.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such, p. 757
cites.quote: “Ye will surely say unto me this proverb: ‘Physician, heal thyself’ ” This was a well known proverb.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This proverb was probably in common use at that time. The meaning is this: Suppose that a man should attempt to heal another when he was himself diseased in the same manner; it would be natural to ask him first to cure himself ... It was only a demand that he would show the proper evidence "by miracles" why they should trust in him
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Such is the meaning of the common proverb, that a physician ought to begin with himself, and those immediately connected with him, before he exhibits his skill in healing others.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: this proverb--like our "Charity begins at home." whatsoever, &c.--"Strange rumors have reached our ears of Thy doings at Capernaum; but if such power resides in Thee to cure the ills of humanity, why has none of it yet come nearer home
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Likely a common saying: the sick need a doctor
notes.about: When the Pharisees complain that His disciples eat with tax collectors and sinners, Jesus answers with what may be a common saying: a doctor is for the sick, not the healthy. The next verse applies it: He came to call sinners to repentance.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick
figure.means: a doctor is for the sick; so Jesus, the doctor of souls, came for sinners who own their need of Him

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke, on the same words in Matthew, to which his note on Luke sends the reader, calls them a common proverb that none could misunderstand or misapply, and says Jesus presents Himself as the Physician of souls, whose healing all need.
notes.limit: The text does not mark the words as a proverb or say whether they were already in common use.

cites.quote: A common proverb, which none could either misunderstand or misapply. ... Jesus Christ represents himself here as the sovereign Physician of souls. 2. That all stand in need of his healing power. 3. That men must acknowledge their spiritual maladies, and the need they have of his mercy, in order to be healed by him.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Jesus pictures Himself as the bridegroom
notes.about: Asked why His disciples eat and drink while others fast, Jesus answers with a picture of a wedding. The guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them; when he is taken from them, they will fast. The picture implies Himself as the bridegroom and His disciples as the guests.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: the guests of the bridegroom
figure.means: Jesus is the bridegroom and His disciples the guests; while He is with them it is a time of joy, and when He is taken from them they will fast

original.note: In Luke's Greek the guests are the sons of the bridechamber, a Hebrew way of naming the guests at a wedding.

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry says the disciples were then as the children of the bride-chamber, and the bridegroom taken away is Christ leaving them. John Calvin, on Matthew, says Jesus compares Himself to the bridegroom, and that children of the bridegroom is a Hebrew phrase for wedding guests. Albert Barnes, on Matthew: the first of Christ's three illustrations is from a marriage, Jesus with His disciples.
notes.limit: The text does not name the bridegroom; the writers take Him to be Jesus, as the picture implies.

cites.quote: Now they were as the children of the bride-chamber, when the bridegroom is with them, when they have plenty and joy, and every day is a festival. ... When Christ shall leave them with their hearts full of sorrow, their hands full of work, and the world full of enmity and rage against them, then shall they fast
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Christ apologizes for his disciples on the score of the season, alleging that God was still pleased to indulge them in joyous feelings, as if they were present at a marriage: for he compares himself to the bridegroom, who enlivens his friends by his presence. ... The children of the bridegroom, or of the nuptial bed, is a Hebrew phrase, which denotes the guests at a marriage.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Christ, in reply to them, used three illustrations ... The first is taken from a marriage. ... I am with my disciples. It is with them a time of joy. It is not fit that they should use the tokens of grief, and fast now. When I am taken away, it will then be proper that they should fast.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A parable: a new patch on an old garment
notes.about: Told that His disciples do not fast as others do, Jesus also tells a parable: no one tears a patch from a new garment to sew on an old one, for the new is torn and the patch does not match the old. Many read it of strict duties such as fasting, laid too soon on those not yet ready to bear them.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: No one tears a piece of cloth from a new garment and sews it on an old one
figure.means: strict duties such as fasting, laid too soon on those not yet ready for them, which would harm them rather than help

notes.evidence: Calvin calls the patch and the wineskins two comparisons, of weak disciples and a discipline too strict for them. Augustine, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas: before the Spirit came the disciples were as old garments. Albert Barnes: making them fast then would be like a new patch on an old garment. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary): fasting is the new patch that does not agree with the old.

cites.quote: He supports the preceding statement by two comparisons, one of which is taken from garments, and the other from vessels of wine ... The comparison is beautifully adapted to the matter in hand, if we explain it as referring to the weak and tender disciples of Christ, and to a discipline more strict than they were able to bear.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.at: Augustine, Questions on the Gospels ii. 18
cites.quote: The gift of the Holy Spirit being received, there is a kind of fast, which is of joy, which they who are already renewed to a spiritual life most seasonably celebrate. Before they receive this gift, He says they are as old garments, to which a new piece of cloth is most unsuitably sewed on, i. e. any part of the doctrine which relates to the soberness of the new life
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

cites.quote: At the proper time all the sterner duties of religion will be properly regarded; but "at present," to teach them to fast when they see "no occasion" for it - when they are full of joy at the presence of their Master - would be like putting a piece of new cloth on an old garment ... It would be ill-timed, inappropriate, and incongruous.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The meaning of the parable in its direct application lies very near the surface. ... The old garment is the common life of sinful men, such as Matthew and his guests; the new garment is the life of holiness, the religious life in its completeness; fasting, as one element of that life, is the patch of new cloth which agrees not with the old
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: A second picture: new wine bursts old wineskins
notes.about: Jesus adds a second picture: new wine poured into old wineskins bursts them, so new wine goes into new skins. Luke alone adds that no one who has drunk old wine wants the new. Many read it of strict duties laid too soon on disciples not yet ready; one takes the new wine as the gospel's freer life.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: no one pours new wine into old wineskins
figure.means: what is new cannot be forced into what is not ready for it; many read it of strict duties laid too soon on disciples not yet ready

notes.evidence: Calvin (Harmony of the Gospels) calls the patch and the wineskins two comparisons, the old skins being weak disciples. Augustine, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas: the apostles are likened to old skins until renewed by the Spirit. Albert Barnes calls verse 39 a proverb: making them fast now is like new wine in old skins. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary): new wine is the gospel's freer life.
notes.limit: The writers differ on verse 39: one takes the old wine as the milder way the disciples had come to know, another as the old religion of the Law, which made men slow to take up the new.

cites.quote: He supports the preceding statement by two comparisons, one of which is taken from garments, and the other from vessels of wine ... when Christ compares his disciples to old bottles and torn garments, he does not mean that they were wasted by long use, but that they were weak and wanted strength.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.at: Augustine, Questions on the Gospels ii. 18
cites.quote: But the Apostles are compared to old skins, who are more easily burst with new wine, i. e. with spiritual precepts, than contain them. ... But they were new skins at that time, when after the ascension of the Lord they received the Holy Spirit, when from desire of His consolation they were renewed by prayer and hope.
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

cites.quote: The meaning of this proverb in this place seems to be this: You Pharisees wish to draw my disciples to the "austere" and "rigid" duties of the ceremonial law - to fasting and painful rites; but they have come under a milder system. ... to teach them to fast when they see "no occasion" for it ... would be like ... new wine into old bottles
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The interpretation of the imagery is not far to seek. The old wine is the principle — in spiritual things, the religion — that animated the man’s former life. In relation to those immediately addressed, it represented the motive-power of the Law in its rigid and Pharisaic form. The new wine, as in the Notes on the previous parables, is the freer, nobler, life-power of the gospel.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: A parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man?”
notes.about: Jesus tells a parable as a question: can a blind man lead a blind man, and will they not both fall into a pit? One who cannot see the truth is no guide for others, and he and those he leads come to ruin together. After His call not to judge (verse 37), it can also warn one who judges others.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Can a blind man lead a blind man?
figure.means: one who cannot see the truth himself cannot guide others to it, and teacher and taught fall into ruin together

original.note: In Luke's Greek the word for parable, parabolē, is wide enough to take in a short saying that holds a likeness, as this one does.

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke says it seems to have been a general proverb: a man cannot teach what he does not understand. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) says Luke uses parable in its wider sense of a proverbial saying holding a likeness, applied here to one who judges another. Cyril of Alexandria, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas, calls it a needful parable for the disciples, the world's future teachers.

cites.quote: This appears to have been a general proverb, and to signify that a man cannot teach what he does not understand. ... A man who is not illuminated from above is utterly incapable of judging concerning spiritual things, and wholly unfit to be a guide to others. ... run the risk of falling into the ditch of perdition himself, together with the unhappy objects of his religious instruction
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: giving an example of the wider sense of the word “parable,” as applicable to any proverbial saying that involved a similitude. ... Here its application is clear enough. The man who judges and condemns another is as the blind leader of the blind.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.at: Cyril of Alexandria, Catena Aurea on Luke 6:39-42
cites.quote: The Lord added to what had gone before a very necessary parable, as it is said, And he spake a parable to them, for His disciples were the future teachers of the world, and it therefore became them to know the way of a virtuous life, having their minds illuminated as it were by a divine brightness, that they should not be blind leaders of the blind.
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

notes.short: A speck in a brother's eye, a beam in your own
notes.about: Jesus goes on with another picture: a man looks at the speck in his brother's eye but does not notice the beam in his own. The speck is a small fault and the beam a great sin. He must first take the beam out of his own eye, and then he will see clearly to help his brother.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: the speck in your brother’s eye, but fail to notice the beam in your own eye
figure.means: a brother's small fault, and the far greater sin a man fails to see in himself, which he must deal with first

notes.evidence: Theophylact, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas, calls it another parable drawn from the same figure, the speck being a slight fault and the beam a great sin. Matthew Henry says it is absurd to spy small faults in others, like a speck in the eye, while not perceiving a beam in one's own, and that we must begin with ourselves.
notes.limit: Luke gives the word parable at verse 39. One writer calls the speck and the beam a further parable; the other gives the likeness without that name.

cites.quote: But the Lord introduces another parable taken from the same figure, as follows, But why seest thou the mote (that is, the slight fault) which is in thy brother’s eye, but the beam which is in thine own eye (that is, thy great sin) thou regardest not?
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

cites.quote: It is very absurd for any to pretend to be so quick-sighted as to spy small faults in others, like a mote in the eye, when they are themselves so perfectly past feeling as not to perceive a beam in their own eye. ... To help to pull the mote out of our brother's eye is a good work, but then we must qualify ourselves for it by beginning with ourselves
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: A good tree and a bad tree, known by their fruit
notes.about: Jesus says no good tree bears bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit: each tree is known by its own fruit, and figs are not picked from thornbushes. So what a man does shows what he is, and verse 45 traces it to the good or evil stored up in his heart, from which the mouth speaks.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: No good tree bears bad fruit
figure.means: what a person does and says shows what he is within, as its fruit shows the kind of tree

notes.evidence: Calvin takes it as a general rule that every man is to be judged by his fruits, as a tree is known by its fruit. Cyril of Alexandria, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas, says good and bad men are known by their works as a tree by its fruits. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) names the likeness of the tree and its fruit, and reads the good heart's fruit as kindness, not harsh judgment.
notes.limit: Luke gives the word parable at verse 39, and the writers call this a likeness. One takes verse 45, the treasure of the heart, as a further figure for the same truth.

cites.quote: This statement, as related by Luke, appears to be a general instruction given by Christ, that by the fruits our opinion of every man ought to be formed, in the same manner as a tree is known by its fruit
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.at: Cyril of Alexandria, Catena Aurea on Luke 6:43-45
cites.quote: But having shewn that the good and the bad man may be discerned by their works as a tree by its fruits, he now sets forth the same thing by another figure, saying, A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

cites.quote: follow on a reproduction of the similitude of the tree and its fruit. The sequence of thought in that passage helps us to trace a like sequence here. Out of the “good treasure of his heart” the good man would bring forth, not harsh or hasty judgment, but kindness, gentleness, compassion
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Two builders: on the rock, or with no foundation
notes.about: Jesus asks why they call Him Lord but do not do what He says, then shows what the one who obeys is like: a man who dug deep and laid his foundation on the rock, so the torrent could not shake his house. The one who hears and does not obey built with no foundation, and his house fell.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: He is like a man building a house
figure.means: one who hears Christ's words and does them stands firm when trial comes; one who only hears them falls, and his ruin is great

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls it a similitude: those who hear His sayings and do them are like a house built on a rock, founding their hope on Christ. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) calls it the parable, the deep digging being a work that goes deep into the life. Cyril of Alexandria, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas, says it shows the gain of keeping the commandments and the loss of disobeying.

cites.quote: This he illustrates by a similitude ... which shows, (1.) That those only make sure work for their souls and eternity ... who do not only come to Christ as his scholars, and hear his sayings but do them ... They are like a house built on a rock. These are they that take pains in religion, as they do,—that dig deep, that found their hope upon Christ, who is the Rock of ages
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Here again the all but verbal reproduction of the parable shows the impression which its repetition had left on the minds of men. … St. Luke alone reports that the wise man “digged deep” … It is not a passing emotion of assurance, a momentary act of faith, but involves a process that goes deep through the surface strata of the life, till it finds a foundation in a purified and strengthened will
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.at: Cyril of Alexandria, Catena Aurea on Luke 6:46-49
cites.quote: But the advantage which arises from the keeping of the commandments, or the loss from disobedience, he shews as follows; Whosoever cometh to me, and heareth my sayings, he is like to a man who built his house upon a rock, &c.
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

notes.short: Children in the market: a generation never pleased
notes.about: Jesus likens the men of His generation to children in the marketplace: some played the flute and sang a dirge, but the others would neither dance nor weep. Verses 33-34 apply it: they found fault with John, who neither ate bread nor drank wine, and with Jesus, who came eating and drinking.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: They are like children sitting in the marketplace
figure.means: the men of that generation, who found fault with John and with Jesus alike and would be pleased by neither

notes.evidence: John Calvin: Jesus employs a comparison probably taken from children's games, charging the scribes with repelling His grace. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott): our Lord likens that evil generation to such children. David Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) sets out the likeness to children who join neither game. Joseph Benson: like children at play, no way could be found to please them.
notes.limit: The writers differ on which children stand for that generation: two take it to be those who will not join in, one those who call to the others and complain.

cites.quote: He does not include all the men of his age, but speaks particularly of the scribes and their followers. He charges them with this reproach, that while the Lord endeavored, by various methods, to draw them to himself, they repelled his grace with incorrigible obstinacy. He employs a comparison, which was probably taken from a common amusement of children
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The comparison is drawn from one of the common amusements of the children of an Eastern city. ... To such a company our Lord likens the evil generation in which He and the Baptist lived. They were loud in their complaints of the Baptist because he would not share their self-indulgent mirth; they were bitter against Jesus
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: As cross, capricious children, invited by their playmates to join them in their amusements, will play with them neither at weddings nor funerals (juvenile imitations of the joyous and mournful scenes of life), so that generation rejected both John and his Master
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Now, to show these Pharisees and lawyers the perverseness of their disposition, in resisting the evidence of John's mission, and the gracious design of God in calling them to repentance by his ministry, he told them they were like children at play, who never do what their companions desire them, but are so froward and perverse that no contrivance can be found to please them.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Flute and dirge, then John and the Son of Man
notes.about: The children's complaint names the flute and then the dirge. The answer takes them in reverse: John the Baptist came neither eating nor drinking, then the Son of Man came eating and drinking. The mournful lines are in the middle, the joyful ones at the ends.

lines.words: We played the flute for you, and you did not dance;
we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.
For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine,
The Son of Man came eating and drinking,

notes.evidence: Boys sets out these verses in four lines: the more severe and mournful in the two inner lines, the dirge and John the Baptist; the more joyful in the outer lines, the flute and the Son of Man.

cites.quote: In b. and b. we have the more severe and mournful dispensation; in a. and a., the more festive and joyous. Those who rejected John the Baptist were like the children who would not weep to their companion's mourning: those who rejected Christ, like the children who would not dance to their companion's music.

notes.short: A story of two debtors answers Simon's thought
notes.about: Jesus answers Simon's unspoken thought with a story: a moneylender forgives two debtors who cannot pay, one owing ten times more. Many read the lender as God and the debtors as the woman and Simon. Jesus draws the point Himself: “he who has been forgiven little loves little.”

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Two men were debtors to a certain moneylender
figure.means: sinners in debt to God, here the sinful woman and Simon: neither can pay, and only God's free pardon can clear the debt

notes.evidence: Clarke and Barnes say the lender stands for God and the debtors for Simon and the woman. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) likens it to Nathan's parable to David and names the same debtors. Calvin says it shows Simon wrong to condemn a woman the heavenly judge has freed; Henry, that Simon is the lesser debtor and the woman the greater. Plumptre (Ellicott) says neither could pay for their sins.
notes.limit: The likeness lies in its main point, that love answers forgiveness. One writer adds that the free cancelling of the debt does not show how God forgives sins, which rests on Christ's atonement.

cites.quote: It is plain that in this parable our Lord means, by the creditor, God, and, by the two debtors, Simon and the woman who was present.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This is not designed to express anything about the way in which God forgives sinners. He forgives - forgives freely, but it is in connection with the "atonement" made by the Lord Jesus. ... It is clear that by the creditor here our Saviour meant to designate God, and by the "debtors," sinners and the woman present. Simon ... was denoted by the one that owed "fifty" pence
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Like Nathan with David, our Lord conceals His home thrust under the veil of a parable, and makes His host himself pronounce upon the case. The two debtors are the woman and Simon

cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The sower: one seed, four kinds of ground
notes.about: Jesus tells of a farmer whose seed falls along the path, on rocky ground, among thorns and on good soil, and only the good soil bears a crop. He explains it in verses 11-15: “The seed is the word of God,” and the four grounds are four kinds of hearers.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: A farmer went out to sow his seed
figure.means: the word of God sown in many hearers, which bears fruit only in hearts that receive it and hold it fast

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry: the heart is soil to the seed of God's word, and the crop answers to the soil. John Calvin: the seed of doctrine, sown far and wide, is not fruitful everywhere. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott), on Matthew's telling, to which he refers: the seed's four ends picture the kinds of hearers. Theophylact, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas: the word falls in different ways on the hearers.

cites.quote: Now from the parable itself, and the explication of it, observe, (1.) The heart of man is as soil to the seed of God's word; it is capable of receiving it, and bringing forth the fruits of it; but, unless that seed be sown in it, it will bring forth nothing valuable. ... (2.) The success of the seeding is very much according to the nature and temper of the soil
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The design of the parable was to inform them, that the seed of doctrine, which is scattered far and wide, is not everywhere productive; because it does not always find a fertile and well cultivated soil.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The classes of hearers who had gathered round Him were represented, roughly and generally, by the four issues of the seed scattered by the sower, and all preachers of the truth, from that day to this, have felt that their own experience has presented analogous phenomena.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: He said not that the sower threw some on the way side, but that it fell by the way side. For he who sows teaches the right word, but the word falls in different ways upon the hearers
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

notes.short: A lamp is lit to give light, not to be hidden
notes.about: Right after explaining the sower, Jesus says no one lights a lamp only to cover it with a jar or put it under a bed; he sets it on a stand so that those who enter can see. Many read the lamp as the light of His word, given not to be hidden but to shine for others.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: No one lights a lamp and covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed
figure.means: the light of His word given to the disciples, meant to be held out to others and not kept hidden

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry: those given the gift must pass it on, as lighted candles. Albert Barnes: His parables were meant to throw light on the truth, which the disciples were to impart. Eusebius, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas: the secrets of the kingdom, told in parables, are like a lamp lit to give light. Adam Clarke: His preaching was meant to enlighten, His parables to make the truth plain.
notes.limit: One writer takes the lamp to be those who have received the word; the others, the word itself. Luke gives the saying again in 11:33.

cites.quote: Those that have received the gift must minister the same. Ministers that have the dispensing of the gospel committed to them, people that have profited by the word and are thereby qualified to profit others, must look upon themselves as lighted candles ... for a candle must not be covered with a vessel nor put under a bed
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: A candle is not lit up to be put immediately under a measure or a bed, where it can give no light. Its design is to give light. So my preaching by parables is not designed to obscure the truth, but to throw light on it. You should understand those parables, and, understanding them, should impart the truth to others also, as a candle throws its beams upon a dark world.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As if He said, As a lantern is lighted that it should give light, not that it should be covered under a bushel or a bed, so also the secrets of the kingdom of heaven when uttered in parables, although hid from those who are strangers to the faith, will not however to all men appear obscure.
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

cites.quote: The design of my preaching is to enlighten men; my parables not being designed to hide the truth, but to make it more manifest.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The plowman who looks back pictures a divided heart
notes.about: A man offers to follow Jesus but first wants to say goodbye at home. Jesus answers with a picture from the field: a man at the plow must keep his eyes ahead, and one who looks back spoils his furrow. So one who sets out after Jesus but still looks back is not fit for God's kingdom.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: puts his hand to the plow and then looks back
figure.means: one who begins to follow Jesus but turns his heart back to the life he left

notes.evidence: Bullinger calls the verse a brief allegory in Figures of Speech. Barnes says a hand on the plow is a proverbial way of saying one takes up a work, and so in religion. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says plowing needs an eye on the furrow, as the work of God needs an undivided heart. Henry and Calvin take looking back as turning to a worldly life and its cares.
notes.limit: One of these writers takes the words as aimed mainly at those called to preach, though he applies them to every follower of Jesus.

cites.quote: “No man having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.” This is a brief allegory.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: To put one's hand to a plow is a proverbial expression to signify undertaking any business. In order that a plowman may accomplish his work, it is necessary to look onward - to be intent on his employment - not to be looking back with regret that he undertook it. So in religion.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As ploughing requires an eye intent on the furrow to be made, and is marred the instant one turns about, so will they come short of salvation who prosecute the work of God with a distracted attention, a divided heart. Though the reference seems chiefly to ministers, the application is general.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: for then he makes balks with his plough, and the ground he ploughs is not fit to be sown; so thou, if thou hast a design to follow me and to reap the advantages of those that do so, yet if thou lookest back to a worldly life again and hankerest after that

cites.quote: They are said to look back, who become involved in the cares of the world, so as to allow themselves to be withdrawn from the right path; particularly, when they plunge themselves into those employments which disqualify them to follow Christ.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The good Samaritan: who proved a neighbor?
notes.about: Asked “And who is my neighbor?”, Jesus tells of a man left half dead by robbers. A priest and a Levite pass by on the other side, but a Samaritan, from a people the Jews hated, binds his wounds and pays for his care. Jesus ends: “Go and do likewise.”

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho
figure.means: our neighbor is anyone in need, even a stranger or an enemy, and we are to show him mercy as the Samaritan did

notes.evidence: John Calvin: the comparison forces the lawyer to own that the greatest stranger is our neighbor. Albert Barnes calls it a beautiful parable that teaches us to do good to all, even to our enemies. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott): its main lesson is that a shared human nature is ground enough for kindness. Joseph Benson: Jesus corrected the lawyer's narrow view of who is a neighbor by a parable.
notes.limit: Many have also seen Christ pictured in the Samaritan; one writer cited here allows that as a further thought, another rejects it. The note keeps to the lesson all of them state.

cites.quote: which the comparison brought forward forces him to confess. The general truth conveyed is, that the greatest stranger is our neighbor, because God has bound all men together, for the purpose of assisting each other. ... To prove this, Christ compares a Samaritan to a priest and a Levite. It is well known what deadly hatred the Jews bore to the Samaritans
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Go, and do thou likewise - Show the same kindness to "all" - to friend and foe ... from this inimitably beautiful parable we may learn: ... 3. That religion requires us to do good to "all" people, however "accidentally" we may become acquainted with their calamities. 4. That we should do good to our enemies.

He convinced him of his mistake by a parable, an ancient, agreeable, and inoffensive method of conveying instruction, very fit to be used in teaching persons who are greatly prejudiced against the truth.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: A friend at midnight: keep on asking
notes.about: Jesus tells of a man who goes to a friend at midnight to borrow bread for a guest. The friend is in bed and will not get up for friendship's sake, but he gives all that is needed “because of the man’s persistence.” Jesus applies it: “Ask, and it will be given to you.”

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Suppose one of you goes to his friend at midnight
figure.means: prayer that perseveres and does not give up: if persistence wins bread from an unwilling friend, much more will God answer those who keep on asking

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry says Jesus speaks it to teach that men ought always to pray and not lose heart. Albert Barnes: all that applies to God in it is that it is right to persevere in prayer. John Calvin calls it a comparison: believers should not be discouraged by delay. David Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): if persistence wins over a churlish man, how much more will prayer prevail with God.
notes.limit: The friend in bed is not a picture of God as unwilling to help: one writer says only the call to persevere applies to God, and another that God, unlike men, is pleased to be asked.

cites.quote: He speaks this parable with the same intent that he speaks that in ... That men ought always to pray, and not to faint. Not that God can be wrought upon by importunity; we cannot be troublesome to him, nor by being so change his counsels. We prevail with men by importunity because they are displeased with it, but with God because he is pleased with it.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This is "not" to be applied to God, as if it were troublesome to him to be sought unto, or as if "he" would ever reply to a sinner in that manner. All that is to be applied to God in this parable is simply that it is proper to "persevere" in prayer.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A divided kingdom answers the charge of Beelzebul
notes.about: Some say Jesus drives out demons by Beelzebul. He answers with a likeness: a kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided house falls. Verse 18 turns it on Satan: “how can his kingdom stand?” Mark says that in this answer Jesus “began to speak to them in parables.”

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste
figure.means: Satan's kingdom, which could not stand if he fought against himself; so the charge that Jesus drives out demons by Satan's power falls

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke, summing up Mark 3, says that when the scribes put His miracles down to Beelzebub, Jesus vindicates Himself by a parable in Mark 3:23-27. Chrysostom, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas, says He answers them from things of every day: a divided house, city or kingdom falls, so if He cast out devils by a devil, their power would perish.
notes.limit: The saying is a short likeness, not a story. It is called a parable here because Mark names this answer so (Mark 3:23).

cites.quote: The multitudes throng him, and the scribes attribute his miracles to Beelzebub, Mar 3:20-22 . He vindicates himself by a parable, Mar 3:23-27 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

For a house and a city if it be divided is quickly scattered to nothing; and likewise a kingdom, than which nothing is stronger. ... If then, says He, I cast out devils by means of a devil, there is dissension among them, and their power perishes.
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

notes.short: A stronger man overpowers the armed strong man
notes.about: A strong man, fully armed, keeps his house and goods secure, until someone stronger attacks and overpowers him, takes away the armor he trusted in, and divides his plunder. The strong man is Satan, and the stronger one is Christ, whose driving out of demons shows that He has overcome him.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: When a strong man, fully armed, guards his house
figure.means: Satan holding men in his power, until Christ, who is stronger, overcomes him and takes from him those he held captive

notes.evidence: Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) counts this and the unclean spirit as two parables, the stronger one being Christ, who dislodges Satan. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott) says the parable appears here in its fuller form and the strong man is Satan. John Calvin calls it a parable: Satan must be overcome by force. Albert Barnes calls it an illustration proving Christ had subdued Satan.
notes.limit: Matthew and Mark tell of binding the strong man; Luke tells of a stronger man who attacks and overpowers him. The writers take them as one saying.

notes.short: An unclean spirit returns with seven worse
notes.about: An unclean spirit leaves a man and finds no rest. It returns to find the house swept clean and put in order, then brings seven spirits more wicked than itself, and the man ends worse than at first. notes.short: Jesus' grieving words over Jerusalem break off
notes.about: Weeping over Jerusalem, Jesus begins, “If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace!” He never says what knowing it would have meant. The sentence breaks off in sorrow, and He turns to what is now hidden from the city's eyes.

figure.name: Aposiopesis
figure.words: If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace
figure.means: the end is left unsaid: how blessed and safe the city would then have been; grief at what is coming cuts the sentence short

original.note: In Luke's Greek the sentence opens with ei, “if,” and nothing follows to finish it; English renders it as a wish.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Luke 19:42 under Aposiopesis, in grief and complaint: the blessing is overwhelmed by the coming tribulation, and the sense would run on to how happy the city would have been. Calvin calls the speech abrupt, strong feeling being only half expressed. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) sees in the broken sentence the deepest sorrow. Henry calls the manner of speaking abrupt.
notes.limit: The writers fill in the unsaid end in different words; the verse itself leaves it unsaid.

notes.short: Budding trees show that summer is near
notes.about: Jesus points to the fig tree and all the trees: when they sprout leaves, anyone can see that summer is near. “So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.” The signs He has just foretold can be read as surely as the leaves.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Look at the fig tree and all the trees
figure.means: the signs Jesus has just foretold, which show that the kingdom of God is near as surely as new leaves show that summer is coming

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke: Jesus illustrated all the facts He had foretold by the simile of a fig tree. Matthew Henry: the disciples might judge the signs of the times as surely as the approach of summer by the budding trees. John Calvin calls it a similitude but takes it as more than a sign that Christ's coming is near: the frail state of the Church is no sign that it is dying.
notes.limit: One writer takes it further: as trees look weaker in spring just before new growth, so the weakness of the Church under trial is no sign that it is dying.
